title: Self-assembled Cuprous Coordination Polymer as a Catalyst for CO2 Electrochemical Reduction into C2 Products
abstract: C2 production with conventional metal complex catalysts has been a significant challenge. Here, we present the electrochemical reduction of CO2 into C2 products such as ethylene and ethanol with high selectivity using a self-assembled cuprous coordination polymer nanoparticle (Cu-SCP). The features of the Cu-SCP catalyst are the arrangement of Cu atoms in close proximity, similar to that in metallic Cu, and a stable Cu(I) oxidation state throughout the reaction due to the coordination of ligands with Cu atoms, which inhibits conversion into Cu metal particles. The Cu-SCP also exhibits activity for C2 production that is superior to that of a Cu metal electrode, without modification of the carbon particles and/or ionomers or continuous flow of the highly alkaline electrolyte, which will simplify the fabrication of a CO2 electrolyzer. The Cu-SCP can be synthesized by a facile process that utilizes a heterogeneous reaction, and the product selectivity can be changed by replacement of the organic ligands, which should open up possibilities for the design of other CO2 reduction catalysts.

KEYWORDS: coordination polymer, CO2 reduction, nanomaterials, metal complex materials, electrochemical catalysis
■ INTRODUCTION The electrochemical conversion of carbon dioxide (CO2) into commercially or energetically high-value chemicals has attracted broad interest for CO2 capture and utilization (CCU) and is promising for the effective utilization of renewable energy with large supply fluctuations and the reduction of CO2 emissions to mitigate global warming.
1 C2 products such as ethylene and ethanol, which have a higher volumetric energy density and commercial value than C1 compounds such as CO, HCOOH, CH4, and CH3OH, 2,3 have applications as fuels, chemical feedstocks, and their intermediates. At present, the production of C2 products is almost exclusively performed using Cu electrodes, and a large reaction current density and high product selectivity have been achieved by optimization of the catalysts4−7 or the reactor configuration.8 Oxide-derived Cu electrodes are reported to exhibit high C2 product selectivity; however, their synthesis requires high temperatures and long heating periods or plasma etching processes.4−7,9 The application of carbon materials and/or ionomers is also utilized to suppress deterioration of the Cu metal catalyst.8,10 Furthermore, it is important to have a flow of a highly alkaline electrolyte at both the cathode and anode sites to maintain the reaction.8,10 An easy approach to molecular modification on the Cu metal catalyst has also been reported;11−15 however, while this approach has the advantage of significantly altering the local environment that plays a role
in C2 production by tuning interactions among reactants/ intermediates, there are still few reported catalysts that can maintain stability during the catalysis reaction.14,15
On the other hand, metal complex molecules are suitable catalysts for the production of two-electron reductants from CO2, such as carbon monoxide and formic acid.
16−18 Metal complex molecules have a superior structure for electron transfer because the environment surrounding the metal atoms is easily modified by ligands. However, electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to obtain C2 products with metal complex catalysts still remains a significant challenge.16−18 There are no reports on metal complex catalysts that can generate C2 products without the formation of Cu metal, and the advantage of metal complexes themselves has not yet been exploited.19−26 For example, Cu complexes19−22 such as Cu−phthalocyanine and Cu−porphyrin complexes have been reported, where the metal sites of these electrocatalysts aggregate during the CO2 reduction reaction, which collapses the structure and produces the equivalent of metal clusters.21 Metal−organic frameworks (MOFs) also change into metal clusters or nanoparticles

(NPs) during the CO2 reduction reaction due to the fragility of their structure.23−26
In the present study, we focused our attention on selfassembled cuprous coordination polymer NPs (Cu-SCPs). CuSCPs consist of halogen-bridged binuclear cuprous complex units (Figure 1). Cu-SCPs can be easily synthesized by a
heterogeneous reaction process27−29 without complicated steps such as those used for oxide-derived Cu electrodes. Cu-SCPs are also well-known as fluorescent materials.28,30 Although Cu-SCPs have never been applied for the reduction of CO2, they have some suitable features as electrocatalysts for the formation of C2 products by CO2 reduction, such as low solubility in both aqueous and organic solvents, controllable structures, and control of the copper oxidation state by changing the ligand, and stabilized proximity of the copper atoms that is presumably suitable for C2 production. Here, highly selective electrochemical C2 production from CO2 using Cu-SCPs is demonstrated, and no significant change in the coordination surrounding copper was observed after the reaction in the ex situ experiment, which suggests there was no conversion of the metal complex into metallic Cu. The selectivity toward C2 production is improved by changing the ligands. Cu-SCPs are simply applied onto a carbon substrate, and high C2 production is maintained without flowing highly alkaline electrolyte. No further processing, such as addition of a mixture of carbon particles and/or ionomers, is required to maintain the reaction. This demonstration represents a new approach to the design of CO2 reduction catalysts.
■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Preparation of Cu-SCPs. Cu-SCPs can be prepared using a previously reported heterogeneous reaction process,27−30 which is a simple procedure compared to the conventional methods used to synthesize MOFs.24 (see Figures S1 and S2 and the Experimental Section in the Supporting Information for details). Briefly, a dispersion of ligand NPs is prepared by the addition of dissolved ligands into a poor solvent (refer to the conventional reprecipitation methods31 to produce organic nanocrystals) and mixing with cuprous bromide solution to introduce metal ions to the ligand NPs.29 In the present study,
various Cu-SCPs with three types of ligands with different numbers of phenyl groups were prepared: [Cu2(μBr)2(PPh3)2(μ-BPY)]n (BPY-SCP), [Cu2(μ-Br)2(PPh3)2(μDPE)]n (DPE-SCP), and [Cu2(μ-Br)2(PPh3)2(μ-DPB)]n (DPB-SCP) (Figure 2a). These designed Cu-SCPs exhibit
different hydrophobicity (Figure S3), which is expected to suppress H2 generation as a side reaction
32,33 to CO2 reduction. The size of each Cu-SCP was estimated to be 100−300 nm from field emission-scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) observations (Figures S4 and S5). The shapes of BPY-SCP, DPE-SCP, and DPB-SCP were rhomboidal, polygonal, and nanorods, respectively, according to the ligand employed.
Evaluation of Cu-SCP Electrodes for CO2 Reduction. The selectivity of Cu-SCP electrodes was assessed by performing electrochemical CO2 reduction reactions. The fabrication of Cu-SCP electrodes was simple in that Cu-SCPs filtered on a PTFE membrane from the colloidal solution could be transferred onto a porous carbon electrode. Each Cu-SCP electrode contained almost the same amount of Cu (Table S1). The CO2 reduction activity of the Cu-SCP electrodes was evaluated in a permeable gas diffusion cell in which CO2 gas was blown into a CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte through the electrode (Figure S6). The cell has two compartments separated by a cation exchange membrane. Electrochemical measurements were conducted with a threeelectrode configuration: the Cu-SCP electrode, Ag/AgCl electrode, and platinum foil were used as working, reference, and counter electrodes, respectively. All applied potentials are
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acscatal.0c01593 ACS Catal. 2020, 10, 10412−10419
10413
described in the potential versus reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) form without IR compensation (Figure S7). Chronoamperometric measurements under an applied potential of −0.94 V (Figure 2b, Table S2) showed that each Cu-SCP electrode had an average current density of ca. −15 mA/cm2 for a 1 h measurement (Figure S8). The highest faradaic efficiency was observed for CH4 production with both DPESCP and DPB-SCP, while H2 production had the highest efficiency with BPY-SCP. C2 products (C2H4 and C2H5OH) were successfully produced over the Cu-SCPs, regardless of the type of metal complex catalyst. In particular, DPB-SCP exhibited the best efficiency for C2 production (C2H4 (the number of electrons required for generation: 12e−), 19.8%; C2H5OH (12e
−), 12.2%). These results suggest that the selectivity toward CO2 reduction over SCPs can be controlled by changing the ligand. Furthermore, the total faradaic efficiency for C2 and CH4 production over DPB-SCP was 72%, which indicates the high CO2 reduction selectivity of DPB-SCP, even in near neutral aqueous media (pH 6.8−7.8). The carbon source for CH4, C2H4, and C2H5OH generated over DPB-SCP was identified as the introduced gaseous CO2 by isotope tracer experiments using 13CO2 (Figure S9). C2 production over Cu-SCPs is considered to be caused by the structure of the coordination polymer, whereby the array of metal complexes realizes an arrangement of Cu atoms in close proximity. Such structures enable the C−C coupling reaction, which is necessary for the production of C2 products by realizing multiple Cu atoms located around the reaction sites, similar to a metal array. The Cu-SCPs also showed higher C2 production selectivity than a conventional electrode of Cu metal sputtered on a carbon paper substrate (Cu/CP) at a potential of −0.94 V, which suggests the advantage of Cu-SCPs as metal complex catalysts (Figures 2b and S10). DPE-SCP had a high CH4 selectivity of over 55%, while BPY-SCP changed to produce mainly H2 at −1.34 V (Figure 2c). DPB-SCP exhibited a pronounced difference in the CO2 reduction reaction at −1.34 V vs RHE, where H2 generation was significantly inhibited and the total current efficiency for CH4, C2H4 and C2H5OH production was over 80%. The turnover numbers (TONs) for CH4, C2H4, C2H5OH, and H2 production observed during the electrochemical reaction using 2 μmol of DPB-SCP for 1 h were 14, 6, 11, and 24, respectively, which suggests that DPB-SCP functions well as a CO2 reduction catalyst. DPB-SCP also showed higher C2 production selectivity than Cu/CP at −1.34 V. The applied potential dependence was examined for DPBSCP (Figures 2d and S11); the rate for the generation of C2 products was low at −0.74 V. The CH4 selectivity was enhanced with the application of a more negative potential, and the highest efficiency was observed around −1.14 V, which then decreased at more negative potentials. The highest efficiencies for C2 production observed at −1.34 V were 19.7% and 33.5% for C2H4 and C2H5OH, respectively. These efficiencies for C2 production, especially for C2H5OH, were higher than those previously reported for metal complex catalysts including MOFs in a similar electrolyte.11,34 The production of C2 products such as C2H4 and C2H5OH with Cu metal electrodes requires more negative potentials than those for CH4 generation,
35,36 and the Cu-SCPs showed the same tendency. Furthermore, the selectivity toward C2H4 production gradually increased with the reaction time (Figure S12). The electrolyte pH was also slightly increased at the end of the reaction. The C−C coupling reaction can be promoted by an
increase of the electrolyte pH.37−40 Experimental40 and simulation38 results have indicated that high pH enhances C2 production by lowering the C−C coupling energy barrier, which makes the potential for CH4 formation more negative and thus suppresses the primary competing reactions for C2 production, i.e., H2 and CH4 generation. These trends in the reaction selectivity of DPB-SCP suggest a similar C−C coupling reaction route, as for the well-discussed process for Cu metal electrodes.
Hydrophobicity and Selectivity of Cu-SCPs Controlled by Changing the Ligands. The hydrophobicity of a Cu metal electrode33 has been reported to contribute to enhancement of the selectivity for CO generation from CO2, while the competitive formate production is simultaneously inhibited. CO is considered to be a crucial intermediate in the formation of multicarbon hydrocarbons because similar product distributions are observed in the direct reduction of CO.38 Therefore, control of the hydrophobicity is an important factor to enhance the selectivity toward multicarbon products. The hydrophobicity of the Cu-SCP can be controlled by changing the part of the bipyridine derivative ligand. Water contact angle measurements (Figure S3) indicated that the hydrophobicity of the Cu-SCPs was enhanced with an increase in the number of phenyl groups inserted at the center of the bipyridine derivative ligand. The faradaic efficiency for H2 production decreased with an increase of the hydrophobicity of the Cu-SCPs, and DPB-SCP with the highest hydrophobicity exhibited the highest selectivity toward C2 production. Therefore, control of the hydrophobicity by changing the ligand is one approach to improving the selectivity for C2 production. In addition, CO2 reduction was performed using highly crystalline bulk particles of DPB (bulk-DPB) and compared with DPB-SCP NPs. Cu NPs can promote the C−C coupling reaction, unlike bulk solid materials such as Cu foil.24,41,42 The DPB-SCP NPs also had enhanced selectivity for C2 production compared to that for the bulk crystalline particles (Figure S13). A distinct difference between the DPBSCP NPs and bulk-DPB was observed in fluorescence spectroscopy measurements. The fluorescence emission maximum of the DPB-SCP NPs was red-shifted compared with that of bulk-DPB (Figure S14). It has been reported that the greater red-shift of the fluorescence emission maximum for DPE-SCP than that for BPY-SCP is caused by the conformational flexibility of the crystal structure and it indicates the ease of structural relaxation during excitation.43 X-ray diffraction (XRD) and infrared (IR) spectroscopy measurements indicated that the fabricated DPB-SCP NPs have a more flexible conformation than BPY-SCP and DPE-SCP, and DPBSCP tends to be more flexible with an increase in the number of phenyl groups inserted at the center of the bipyridine derivative ligand (Figures S15−S20). It is considered that the conformational flexibility of the DPB-SCP NPs is one of the factors that results in better performance for C2 production than bulk-DPB, which is a highly crystalline coordination polymer, or BPY-SCP and DPE-SCP. Therefore, Cu-SCPs have an advantage in that CO2 reduction can be controlled by changing the organic ligands, not only to suppress H2 generation by changing the hydrophobicity but also to enhance C2 product selectivity by a more pronounced ligand effect due to conformational flexibility, unlike previously reported metal complex catalysts.
Oxidation State of Copper for Cu-SCP. The oxidation state of copper in the Cu-SCPs was evaluated using X-ray
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acscatal.0c01593 ACS Catal. 2020, 10, 10412−10419
10414
photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) measurements. XPS Cu 2p3/2 peaks of the Cu-SCPs were observed at approximately 932 eV (Figure 3a), which could indicate Cu(0) or Cu(I).5,44 In addition, the Cu LMM peaks obtained by XPS were at approximately 571 eV (Figure 3b). Cu(0) and Cu(I) show peaks at approximately 568 and 570 eV, respectively; therefore, the Cu LMM peaks observed from the Cu-SCPs can be assigned to Cu(I).44 Cu(I) species are thus present at the surface of the Cu-SCPs. Cu K-edge XANES spectra (Figures 3c and S21) indicate that the Cu-SCPs have a well-matched absorption end point and a first inflection point with the Cu2O reference, which suggests that the Cu atoms in the Cu-SCPs exist mostly in the monovalent state. Both experimental and theoretical results have suggested that oxide-derived Cu catalysts including Cu(I) enhance the selectivity toward C2 products, and the active species for the generation of C2 products is considered to be Cu(I).4−7,9 On the other hand, BPY-SCP with low selectivity toward C2 production also includes Cu(I), which suggests that the important factor for C2 production with Cu-SCPs is not only the presence of Cu(I) but also suitable ligands surrounding the Cu atoms, which control the electron density around the Cu atoms. XPS Br 3d spectra showed that the peak position for all the Cu-SCPs shifted to the lower energy side compared to that for only CuBr (Figure S22). This peak shift occurs when an electrondonating ligand, in this case PPh3, coordinates to a metal-Br species.45 Therefore, it is considered that Cu in each Cu-SCP is coordinated to PPh3, which suggests that all three Cu-SCPs with different ligands form metal complex structures. The turnover frequency (TOF) of DPB-SCP having Cu(I) was examined from a kinetics viewpoint and compared with previously reported Cu metal electrodes with molecular tuning.11−14 The TOF of DPB-SCP is smaller than that of Cu−Cu2O-1/Cu-foil11 (Table S3). However, the TOF of DPB-SCP for C2 production is superior to that of Cu−Cu2O1/CP, in which Cu−Cu2O-1 is modified on the carbon paper (Table S3). Furthermore, there is no other example of a metal complex catalyst that produces ethanol with high selectivity. The structure of the Cu-SCPs can stabilize Cu(I), and it is
expected that the TOF will be improved by optimization of the ligands and electrolysis conditions.
Comparison of CO2 Reduction Selectivity between DPB-SCP and Cu Metal under Long-Time Reaction. The selectivity of CO2 reduction with DPB-SCP was compared with that for a conventional Cu metal electrode during a longtime reaction in a two-compartment cell separated by an anion exchange membrane. The DPB-SCP cathode could generate H2, CH4, and C2H4 at the start of the reaction (Figure 4). The current efficiency for C2H4 production was gradually increased with the reaction time, while H2 and CH4 production decreased. The time course for partial current density for various reductants (Figure S23) indicated that the increase in cathodic current mainly contributed to the generation of C2H4. It was found that the partial current for H2 was constant and that for CH4 gradually decreased, while only the partial current density for C2H4 increased with time over the 10 h of measurement. This time course for C2H4 and CH4 observed for DPB-SCP is opposite to that reported for Cu-MOF changed into a Cu cluster catalyst,25 which suggests a different reaction mechanism from the Cu cluster catalyst. On the other hand, the Cu metal electrode exhibited high current efficiency for H2 production compared with DPB-SCP and it increased with time. CH4 and C2H4 were also detected at the start of the reaction; however, the current efficiencies for CH4 and C2H4 production were decreased with time, and the amounts produced were negligible at the end of the reaction. There have been some reports on a CO2 electrolyzer that combine a Cu metal electrode with an anion exchange membrane. Although these cells can produce C2 products with high current efficiency, they are operated with continuous electrolyte flow for both catholyte and anolyte, which is necessary to maintain the electrodes under the same reaction conditions.8,10,46−50 On the other hand, DPB-SCP can continuously generate C2 products for 10 h without an electrolyte flow. Furthermore, it has been suggested that conventional copper metal catalysts are easily decomposed and eluted during the electrochemical reaction, so that the active species for C2 generation would disappear from the reaction surface.7
Therefore, previously reported Cu metal electrodes were
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acscatal.0c01593 ACS Catal. 2020, 10, 10412−10419
10415
prepared by compounding Cu metal with carbon particles and/or ionomers for stabilization.8 In the case of DPB-SCP, no significant change in the Cu and Br state was observed after the reaction (Figures 3d−f and S24−S26). FT-IR and FE-SEM results also showed no significant change in the ligands or the catalyst shape (Figures S27 and S28). In addition, bright-field TEM observations of DPB-SCP after a 10 h reaction were conducted, and no dark spots that would indicate the formation of Cu clusters were observed (Figure S29). Balamurugan et al.51 recently reported that the presence of Cu clusters in a molecular Cu complex catalyst was confirmed by bright-field TEM observation, although it could not be confirmed from XANES and XPS measurements. Therefore, both ex situ spectroscopic analysis and morphological observations suggest that the valence, electronic states, and ligand states of DPB-SCP are not significantly changed after the reaction. A stable environment for Cu(I) is formed by the ligands surrounding the Cu atom, and this is the first example of high C2 production selectivity over a long-time reaction without compounding Cu metal with carbon particles and/or ionomers. The generation of C2H4 and the suppression of H2 and CH4 production have been reported with an increase in the local pH without electrolyte flow.40 On the other hand, it has been suggested that bicarbonate equilibrium conditions become unfavorable with an increase of the local pH during CO2 reduction, which causes a significant decrease in performance due to CO2 depletion and a decrease in gas
diffusion capacity.34,50,52 Garcia de Arquer et al.10 recently reported that the partial current density for C2H4 production on a Cu metal catalyst with a hydrophilic surface10 was significantly improved by the introduction of perfluorinated sulfonic acid ionomers having both hydrophobic and hydrophilic functionalities, along with ion transport. The mechanism for the enhancement of CO2 reduction is considered to be the effective supply of gaseous CO2 through the hydrophobic layer of the ionomer and an improvement of the ion transfer with the ionomer compared to the electrolyte. It is considered that the DPB-SCP NPs have the same effect as the modification of carbon particles and/or ionomer to stabilize the Cu atoms. It is surmised that this is the reason that DPB-SCP maintained high selectivity, even under electrolysis conditions that were unfavorable for a bare Cu metal electrode. This is one of the unique features of Cu-SCPs as CO2 reduction catalysts and why a simple CO2 electrolyzer could be realized without modification of the electrode or electrolyte flow. We surmised a mechanism of the increase in the partial current density of C2H4. At this time, the mechanism with Cu as a reference40 suggests that CH4 is generated in the initial state with few multiple *CO intermediates, and C2H4 is generated by the increase of *CO intermediates that are located in the adjacent region during the reaction and facilitate the C−C coupling reaction. The coexistence of two different pathways for ethylene formation has been reported.40,53 The coupling of two *CO molecules is caused at the low overpotential pathway, while CO protonation is caused at the high overpotential pathway. The increase in total current is considered to be caused by an increase in the concentration of the intermediate (*CO) and facilitates the C−C coupling reaction that contributes to the production of C2H4, which has a lower Gibbs energy than CH4.
53 In fact, the increase of the partial current density of CO is related to the increase of C2H4 (Figure S23), though the production of CH4 is reduced. It has been previously reported that the oxidation state of the central Cu atom in Cu−phthalocyanine and Cu−porphyrin complexes, the chloride-bridged dicopper(II) complex, and MOFs was changed to Cu(0) during the CO2 reduction reaction, so that the reactivity of the catalyst was thus changed.21,25 Cu(I)-SCPs clearly exhibit superior activity for C2H5OH formation over that with Cu(0) or Cu(II) metal complex catalysts. On the other hand, the stability of DPB-SCP is a crucial factor for maintaining the superiority of the metal complex, such as the ligand effect. Cu-SCPs are novel materials that clearly have the advantages of metal complex catalysts over metal catalysts in that the selectivity can be easily and significantly changed with a change in the electronic state of the metal complex.
■ CONCLUSIONS Cu-SCPs are the first examples in which improvement of C2 production during the CO2 reduction reaction has been achieved by changing the ligand of the metal complex. C2 products can be generated with high selectivity while maintaining the Cu(I) oxidation state during the reaction, i.e., without conversion of the catalyst into metal NPs, as with conventional metal complex catalysts. The Cu-SCPs exhibit higher activity than a Cu metal electrode, and the current efficiency for C2 production gradually increased with time during a long-term experiment. Cu-SCPs have the advantages of both molecular and metal catalysts in that the environment surrounding the metal atom can be easily tuned by changing
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acscatal.0c01593 ACS Catal. 2020, 10, 10412−10419
10416
the type of ligand, where the reaction selectivity toward C2 products or CH4 can be changed. Cu-SCPs are also considered to create a desirable environment for the diffusion of gaseous CO2 without requiring further modification such as mixing with carbon materials and/or ionomers. Further investigation of Cu-SCPs is expected to clarify the factors at play in the enhancement of CO2 reduction selectivity, such as the oxidation state of the metal and the number and distance of metal atoms required for an effective reaction. This work presents a simple approach to the efficient transformation of CO2 into valuable chemicals or liquid fuels, and the results given here will be helpful for the design of novel catalysts. We expect that this work will trigger many interesting studies on the development of CO2 reduction electrocatalysts in the future.
